reconcile.note: Keil and Delitzsch read the difference as procedural: God personally avenged Cain's murder, then later delegated that vengeance to human courts.

discrepancy.note: Wellhausen reads Genesis 9:6's blood-vengeance law as the Priestly Code's revision of the older Yahwist notion in Genesis 4, of which this pair is one instance.

quotes.text: vengeance for the spilling of blood is not the affair of the relatives but the affair of God; and that it is demanded for man as man, whether master or slave, and no money compensation allowed. … Yet the religious notion of HUMANITY underlying this sentence is not ancient with the Hebrews any more than with other nations; cf. Genesis iv. 15, 24, and Exodus xxi. 20 seq.
quotes.attr: Julius Wellhausen (d. 1918), Prolegomena to the History of Israel (1885), on the Priestly Code's blood-vengeance law versus the earlier Yahwist notion in Genesis 4.

sides.snippet: whoever slays Cain, vengeance will be taken on him sevenfold
sides.verseText: Yahweh said to him, \"Therefore whoever slays Cain, vengeance will be taken on him sevenfold.\" Yahweh appointed a sign for Cain, lest any finding him should strike him.

sides.snippet: Whoever sheds man's blood, by man will his blood be shed
sides.verseText: Whoever sheds man's blood, by man will his blood be shed, for in the image of God made he man.
